# In Defense of Useless Knowledge

There is a species of fact that serves no purpose whatsoever, and I have come to believe these are among the most valuable things a mind can hold. Consider: honey never spoils. Archaeologists opening Egyptian tombs thousands of years old have found sealed pots of honey inside, still perfectly edible after three millennia. No one needs to know this. It will not help you file your taxes, negotiate a raise, or parallel park. And yet something in me loosens when I learn it, the way a body loosens in warm water—as though the world had just been revealed to be slightly more generous than advertised.

Take the octopus, which tastes with its skin. Every sucker on every arm is dense with chemoreceptors, so when an octopus touches a rock, it learns what the rock feels like and what it tastes like in the same instant. Better yet, two-thirds of an octopus's neurons reside not in its brain but in its arms; each arm is, in some meaningful sense, thinking for itself—a committee of eight semi-independent minds sharing one coat. Meanwhile the wombat—round, placid, apparently unbothered by any concern whatsoever—produces cube-shaped droppings. Biologists believe the shape keeps the pellets from rolling off the rocks where wombats leave them to mark territory. Evolution, presented with the problem of scat placement, chose geometry.

Even our vocabulary hides treasure. Petrichor—the smell of rain arriving on dry earth—was only named in 1964, by two Australian scientists who built it from the Greek *petra*, stone, and *ichor*, the golden blood of the gods. The scent itself comes largely from geosmin, a compound manufactured by soil bacteria, and the human nose can detect it at concentrations measured in parts per trillion. We are, quite literally, built to notice when the ground begins to drink. Someone, somewhere, decided this sensation deserved a name—and the naming waited until the twentieth century. What else are we still waiting to name?

Then there are the facts that quietly rearrange your sense of time. Cleopatra lived closer in history to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid of Giza. Sharks are older than trees: sharks have patrolled the oceans for roughly 450 million years, while trees only managed to stand upright about 350 million years ago. For nearly a hundred million years, the seas were ruled by creatures older than forests. Oxford University was teaching students for centuries before the Aztec Empire was founded. Hold these facts together and history stops being a straight line and becomes a landscape—deep with unexpected valleys, crowded with neighbors who never knew they overlapped.

The planets keep their own oddities. Venus rotates backward, and so slowly that its day outlasts its year; sunrise to sunrise on Venus takes longer than a full trip around the sun. Saturn is less dense than water—if you could find a bathtub of appropriate size, the planet would float in it. Uranus, for reasons astronomers still debate, rolls around the sun on its side like a dropped marble. None of this helps anyone get anywhere. All of it makes the sky feel less like a ceiling and more like a cabinet of curiosities left slightly open.

And then there are the tender ones. Sea otters hold hands while they sleep, so the current won't drift them apart. A group of flamingos is called a flamboyance, which may be the most honest word in the English language. The shortest war in recorded history, between Britain and Zanzibar in 1896, lasted under forty-five minutes—meaning there exists a war shorter than a lunch break, a conflict you could have missed entirely by stepping out for coffee and returning to find the treaty signed.

A reasonable person might ask: what are these *for*? The honest answer is: nothing. But I want to push back gently on the question itself, because the assumption that knowledge must justify itself through usefulness is a kind of poverty. Utility is a fine servant and a terrible master. If every thought must earn its keep, the mind becomes a warehouse, and warehouses are optimized for storage, not life. The useless fact is a small act of leisure performed by the intellect—leisure in the old sense, the sense that gave us the word *school*, from the Greek *scholē*, which originally meant free time. Learning began as what people did when they were finally free to do nothing useful at all.

There is also a practical case hiding inside the impractical one, which is that wonder behaves like a muscle. The person who practices being astonished by a wombat's cubic output is exercising the same faculty that lets them be astonished by a stranger's kindness or a city at dusk. Attention is not a fixed quantity; it is a habit, and habits generalize. Delight, practiced deliberately on small and pointless objects, stays available for large and important ones. I suspect much of what we call burnout is really the atrophy of this muscle—the inability to be interested in anything that isn't required.

Curiosity, moreover, turns out to be empathy's rehearsal space. To wonder about an octopus's distributed mind, or the private chemistry of soil bacteria, is to practice the fundamental posture of not-knowing: the willingness to let the world be stranger than your model of it. That posture transfers. People who can hold genuine uncertainty about cephalopods tend to be better at holding it about each other. The habit of asking *what is it like to be that?*—a question philosophers once reserved for other minds—begins, for many of us, with smaller creatures and stranger questions.

So here is my modest proposal: hoard useless facts the way misers hoard coins, and spend them recklessly. Keep them in the glovebox of the mind for traffic jams and long lines and awkward silences. Offer them to children, who understand immediately that a cube-producing wombat is excellent news. And the next time rain arrives after a dry spell and the whole street suddenly smells like stone and iron and something ancient waking up, remember that you are detecting a bacterial perfume at parts per trillion—that your body, without any training at all, knows how to celebrate weather.

Somewhere in Egypt, in a sealed clay pot, three-thousand-year-old honey is still sweet. It is needed by no one. It is offered to everyone. That, I think, is exactly what useless knowledge is: sweetness preserved past all reason, waiting patiently in the dark for whoever might come along and simply want it.

**In Defense of Useless Knowledge**

There is a species of fact that serves no purpose whatsoever, and I have come to believe these are among the most valuable things a mind can hold. Consider: honey never spoils. Archaeologists opening Egyptian tombs thousands of years old have found sealed pots of honey inside, still perfectly edible after three millennia. No one needs to know this. It will not help you file your taxes, negotiate a raise, or parallel park. And yet something in me loosens when I learn it, the way a body loosens in warm water—as though the world had just been revealed to be slightly more generous than advertised.

(~110 words)

Take the octopus, which tastes with its skin. Every sucker on every arm is dense with chemoreceptors, so when an octopus touches a rock, it learns what the rock feels like and what it tastes like in the same instant. Better yet, two-thirds of an octopus's neurons reside not in its brain but in its arms; each arm is, in some meaningful sense, thinking for itself, a committee of eight semi-independent minds wearing one coat. Meanwhile the wombat—round, placid, apparently unbothered by all concerns—produces cube-shaped droppings. Biologists believe the shape keeps the pellets from rolling off the rocks where wombats leave them to mark territory. Evolution, presented with the problem of scat placement, chose geometry.

(~125 words)

Even our vocabulary hides treasure. Petrichor—the smell of rain arriving on dry earth—was only named in 1964, by two Australian scientists who built it from the Greek petra, stone, and ichor, the golden blood of the gods. The scent itself comes largely from geosmin, a compound manufactured by soil bacteria, and the human nose can detect it at concentrations measured in parts per trillion. We are, quite literally, built to notice when the ground begins to drink. Someone, somewhere, decided this sensation deserved a name, and the naming took until the twentieth century. What else are we still waiting to name?

(~105 words)

Then there are the facts that quietly rearrange your sense of time. Cleopatra lived closer in history to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid of Giza. Sharks are older than trees: sharks have patrolled the oceans for roughly 450 million years, while trees only managed to stand upright about 350 million years ago. For nearly a hundred million years, the seas were ruled by creatures older than forests. Oxford University was already teaching students for centuries before the Aztec Empire was founded. Hold these facts together and history stops being a straight line and becomes a landscape—deep with unexpected valleys, crowded with neighbors who never knew they overlapped.

(~120 words)

The planets keep their own oddities. Venus rotates backward, and so slowly that its day outlasts its year; sunrise to sunrise on Venus takes longer than a full trip around the sun. Saturn is less dense than water—if you could find a bathtub of appropriate size, the planet would float in it, leaving a ring-shaped stain. Uranus, for reasons astronomers still debate, rolls around the sun on its side like a dropped marble. None of this helps anyone get anywhere. All of it makes the sky feel less like a ceiling and more like a cabinet of curiosities left slightly open.

(~110 words)

And then there are the tender ones. Sea otters hold hands while they sleep, so that the current won't separate them from one another. A group of flamingos is called a flamboyance, which may be the most honest word in the English language. The shortest war in recorded history, between Britain and Zanzibar in 1896, lasted somewhere between thirty-eight and forty-five minutes—meaning there exists a war shorter than a lunch break, a conflict you could have missed entirely by stepping out for coffee and returning to find the treaty signed.

(~95 words)

A reasonable person might ask: what are these for? And the honest answer is: nothing. But I want to push back gently on the question itself, because the assumption that knowledge must justify itself through usefulness is a kind of poverty. Utility is a fine servant and a terrible master. If every thought must earn its keep, then the mind becomes a warehouse, and warehouses are optimized for storage, not life. The useless fact is a small act of leisure performed by the intellect—leisure in the old sense, the sense that gave us the word school, from the Greek scholē, which meant leisure. Learning began as what people did when they were finally free to do nothing useful at all.

(~120 words)

There is also a practical case hiding inside the impractical one, which is that wonder behaves like a muscle. The person who practices being astonished by a wombat's cubic output is exercising the same faculty that lets them be astonished by a stranger's kindness or a city at dusk. Attention is not a fixed quantity; it is a habit, and habits generalize. Delight, practiced deliberately on small and pointless objects, stays available for large and important ones. I suspect that much of what we call burnout is actually the atrophy of this muscle—the inability to be interested in anything that isn't required.

(~110 words)

Curiosity, moreover, turns out to be empathy's rehearsal space. To wonder about an octopus's distributed mind, or the private chemistry of soil bacteria, is to practice the fundamental posture of not-knowing: the willingness to let the world be stranger than your model of it. That posture transfers. People who can hold genuine uncertainty about cephalopods tend to be better at holding it about each other. The habit of asking "what is it like to be that?"—a question philosophers once reserved for other minds—begins, for many of us, with smaller creatures and stranger questions.

(~100 words)

So here is my modest proposal: hoard useless facts the way misers hoard coins, and spend them recklessly. Keep them in the glovebox of the mind for traffic jams and long lines and awkward silences. Offer them to children, who understand immediately that a cube-producing wombat is excellent news. And remember, next time rain arrives after a dry spell and the whole street suddenly smells like stone and iron and something ancient waking up, that you are detecting a bacterial perfume at parts per trillion—that your body, without any training at all, knows how to celebrate weather. Somewhere in Egypt, in a sealed clay pot, three-thousand-year-old honey is still sweet. It is needed by no one. It is offered to everyone. That, I think, is exactly what useless knowledge is: sweetness preserved past all reason, waiting patiently in the dark for whoever might come along and simply want it.
